Zcash · private markets · intents

Intents signed and sealed with post-quantum keys, settled in shielded ZEC.

Why: the address you receive at is paid from the solver’s liquidity, never from the wallet you fund with, and the order itself is signed and sealed with post-quantum keys. You sign an intent with ML-DSA-65 and seal it to the solver with ML-KEM-768, escrow testnet ZEC, and a verifier releases or refunds the escrow. Every decision is a signed, hash-chained log entry, anchored in a shielded memo. Zcash spends stay elliptic-curve; the post-quantum part is the intent layer.

The bar under “Deliver ≥” is the share of the escrow the solver must deliver. Solver spread is escrow minus delivery (20,000 on every intent). A release or a refund pays the escrow minus a 15,000 zat fee budget. For A–D (escrow 60,000, deliver 40,000) a release is 45,000 and the solver nets 5,000 over what it delivered; a refund returns 45,000 of the 60,000 (the user loses 15,000, a quarter). For E (escrow 40,000, deliver 20,000) the release was 25,000, again 5,000 over the delivery; a refund would have returned 25,000 of the 40,000 (the user loses 15,000, 37.5%). The part of the fee budget the payout transaction does not spend stays in the escrow wallet, which the verifier holds. A, B and C were funded together in 1d6b3868…; D, in pass 2, in be265ece…; E, by the agent in pass 3, in 3ba64090….

Sign

ML-DSA-65 over the canonical intent; the key id is inside it.

Seal

ML-KEM-768 + HKDF + AES-256-GCM to the solver's key.

Settle

Shielded funding, fill and payout, each read with a viewing key.

Sign the decision

The verifier's ML-DSA-65 log, hash-chained and anchored.

What is post-quantum, and what is not

Post-quantum

  • The intent signature (ML-DSA-65)
  • The sealed envelope to the solver (ML-KEM-768): recording it today does not open it later
  • The verifier's signatures on every decision

Not post-quantum, and not private

  • Zcash spends and note encryption: a future quantum adversary holding the chain could read the funding and fill memos and link them
  • The escrow’s full viewing key is published, so anyone sees today every funding (amount, intent hash) and every payout out of the escrow: the recipient and amount of each release and refund, including the user’s refund address next to pqi1:<hash>:refund

Limits

read before trusting it
  • Not trustless. The verifier holds the escrow and could withhold a payout. It cannot change the record without the signatures, links or anchors showing it.
  • The solver and the verifier read the plaintext intent. One receive address served all four intents (A–D), so those deliveries can be linked; E, submitted by the agent, got an address of its own. A new address does not unlink one user’s intents: every settled or refunded entry in the public log names the user’s key id and nonce, and the escrow’s viewing key shows the same refund address on each refund.
  • The escrow’s full viewing key is published for auditability: it shows every payout’s recipient and amount, not only the fundings.
  • Anchors are periodic, and each names the one before it. Every anchor the escrow sent can be listed, and a second head, an anchor that names none, or one off the chain fails the check; entries after the last anchor are not covered. Funding and fills need 3 confirmations.
  • ZEC only, testnet only, a single verifier key, not audited. A portfolio piece: the Zecathon entry is Shielded x402.
